Experimental: a starting point for your own judgment. Vendor documentation and your rehearsals decide. Rehearse on lab machines before you run these on a network you're responsible for.

0 · Kickoff, all cells together

Team: a team lead plus one or more people per cell. A cell of three or more names a cell lead, who gathers the cell's files and sends one roll-up to the team lead.

  • P1
    Written authorization: hosts and subnets in scope, change approver, change window, and the owner to call. Note the start time.
  • P1
    Required-services list from the owner: each business app, its host, port, and users; remote access and vendor links. Every step that names the required list reads from this list.
  • P1
    Split each cell's hosts among its people: list them in the cell's Hosts bar with who holds each, and name a cell lead in each cell of three or more.
  • P1
    Agree on management subnets, jump host, NTP source, and syslog collector (the Cisco cell builds ACLs from these).
  • P1
    Team vault for every new secret, plus one shared change log. Sync points: kickoff done · credentials cut over · firewall and ACL changes announced · freeze (the team lead sets the times on the Collab Tab).
  • P1
    Departed admins: names, named accounts, shared accounts they used, and devices they held.
  • P1
    Secrets the old team knew, each with an owner cell; rotate in Phase 3:
SecretCell
AD admins, krbtgt, DSRM, service accounts, local Administrator, backup console, RADIUS shared secretsWindows
root / sudo / wheel, SSH keys, database and app secrets*nix
enable and device users, SNMP, TACACS+/RADIUS keys, VPN pre-shared keys, Wi-Fi keysCisco
hypervisor hosts, BMC (out-of-band management), NAS, ISP and domain-registrar portals, cloud and email admins, security and remote-management consolesassign at kickoff

Experimental: a starting point for your own judgment. Vendor documentation and your rehearsals decide. Rehearse on lab machines before you run these on a network you're responsible for.

Windows Takeover Checklist

Windows 11 (24H2–25H2) · Windows Server 2022 / 2025 · Active Directory. For the Windows cell of a takeover team (a team lead plus one or more people per cell; a cell of three or more names a cell lead) inheriting a network whose last admin team left under a negligence finding.

Situation. Treat every secret the old team held as known to outsiders, and every setting as unreviewed. Work in an elevated PowerShell 5.1 window.

Solo: domain first (it reaches every host), P1 lines in order, P2 when on schedule. Cell of two or more: split the hosts in the Hosts bar, one person on the domain and DCs and the others on servers and workstations; each person reads the line aloud, logs the change, and checks the → read-back. A cell of three or more names a cell lead, who sends the cell's roll-up to the team lead.

Key: P1 = inside the team clock · P2 = when on schedule · P3 = week-1 plan · → = expected read-back · <x> = your value · GUI+ = the GUI is faster here · ⚠︎ and an orange bar = untested on a real system: use with caution, at your own risk · a line without them = run cleanly on a real system.

Rules: evidence before change · disable before delete · a console session (VM console or BMC) stays open for any remote-access change · keep every required service running · one change, one log line (time, host, change, old → new, undo).

2 · Start the long jobs

Domain: start the "Takeover Baseline – Workstations" GPO here, linked at the workstation OUs (or filtered to workstations), so servers and DCs stay outside it. The update-blocker, local-group, Windows LAPS, Defender, firewall, RDP, and SMB settings join it as you reach them, with the Guest account status at Disabled (Security Options), and domain policy carries them to every workstation at the next refresh. A policy left unconfigured leaves a value written by hand on a host in place, so these settings undo local tampering only when set explicitly: Defender's local administrator merge behavior for lists at Disabled (exclusions added through Set-MpPreference on a host stop applying); Defender's Path, Extension, and Process Exclusions set explicitly (Enabled with the approved entries alone, or Disabled), since exclusions written by hand under the Policies key read as policy; Defender's "Turn off Microsoft Defender Antivirus" and "Turn off real-time protection" at Disabled; Windows Update's intranet update location (Disabled, or Enabled with your own WSUS server) with automatic updates on; and the Windows Update service (wuauserv) at Manual under System Services. Servers and DCs, and the other workstation steps, run host by host or through remote shells; with domain policy alone, the hands-on sample takes those other workstation steps by hand, the workstations past it take the Phase 3 cut-off from this GPO on the day (the listed local accounts disabled, the listed remote-control tools blocked by inbound and outbound firewall rules, and a restart, targeted to leave out the sample, that ends live sessions), and their remaining steps go into the week-1 plan. With only a few workstations past the sample, taking the cut-off by hand on them can finish sooner than building these pieces; the estimate's Workstations list says which it counts.

  • P1
    Update blockers: reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate /s39⚠︎ → an unexplained WUServer or NoAutoUpdate=1 is a finding; delete it (Phase 1 saved the state). Then Set-Service wuauserv -StartupType Manual; Start-Service wuauserv40 41⚠︎.
  • P1
    GUI+ Settings > Windows Update42 > Check for updates (Server Core: sconfig43⚠︎, option 6). Restarts wait for Phase 8 or the change window.
  • P1
    WSUS server, when present: the Oct 23, 2025 out-of-band update or later is installed (CVE-2025-59287, actively exploited), and TCP 8530/8531 stay internal.
  • P1
    Defender: Update-MpSignature; Start-MpScan -ScanType QuickScan -AsJob44 45⚠︎ (Server without Defender: Install-WindowsFeature Windows-Defender46⚠︎). → Get-MpComputerStatus | fl AMRunningMode,RealTimeProtectionEnabled,IsTamperProtected47 shows Normal, True, and True on Windows 11 (servers report tamper protection True only under central Defender management). A third-party EDR puts Defender in Passive; confirm that EDR console logs in as your team.

3 · Cut off the old team

Domain (whoever holds the DCs)

  • P1
    Disable each departed admin's accounts now; delete after the HR/legal hold. Disable-ADAccount <sam>48⚠︎ → (Get-ADUser <sam>).Enabled21⚠︎ is False.
  • P1
    Privileged groups hold the approved list only (read priv.csv): Remove-ADGroupMember '<group>' -Members <sam> -Confirm:$false49⚠︎. Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins stay empty apart from one break-glass account.
  • P1
    New vault passwords for every remaining privileged account, the built-in Administrator (RID 500), and shared admin accounts:
    Set-ADAccountPassword <sam> -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'New password')50⚠︎
  • P1
    krbtgt reset 1 of 2 (voids forged tickets), once repadmin /replsummary25⚠︎ shows zero failures. AD swaps whatever you type for a strong random value; each read-only DC has its own krbtgt_<number>. Reset 2 goes in the week-1 plan, at least 10 hours later.
    Set-ADAccountPassword krbtgt -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'Any value')50⚠︎
  • P1
    DSRM password, each DC: ntdsutil "set dsrm password" "reset password on server null" q q51⚠︎.
  • P1
    Service accounts: rotate each one whose service you can update today (set the new password on that service right after); list the rest with owners for week 1.
    Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -like '*'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName,PasswordLastSet | ft Name,PasswordLastSet21⚠︎
  • P1
    Rotate the rest of your kickoff rows: backup console, RADIUS shared secrets (with the Cisco cell), and any hypervisor or BMC rows assigned to you.

Every host (each person on their own hosts)

  • P1
    Local Administrators and Remote Desktop Users hold the approved list only (an orphaned SID makes the cmdlet fail; net localgroup Administrators5 still lists the group):
    Get-LocalGroupMember -SID S-1-5-32-544; Get-LocalGroupMember -SID S-1-5-32-55552⚠︎
    Remove-LocalGroupMember -SID S-1-5-32-544 -Member '<name>'53⚠︎
  • P1
    Local Administrator password: Windows LAPS hosts Reset-LapsPassword54⚠︎; others Get-LocalUser | ? SID -like '*-500' | Set-LocalUser -Password (Read-Host -AsSecureString)4 55⚠︎ host by host, each with a password of its own for the vault (one run of that line across hosts would give every host the same password). Workstations that domain policy reaches take the Windows LAPS policy in the workstation baseline (once per domain: the LAPS schema update and the computers' permission to update their own passwords on their OU); each then sets and backs up a password of its own at its next policy refresh, and one that already holds a LAPS password rotates at that refresh once an admin session with the LAPS module and directory rights sets its LAPS password expiration to now (the line below). Through remote shells, the LAPS reset runs on the LAPS hosts in one pass. Guest stays off: Get-LocalUser | ? SID -like '*-501' | Disable-LocalUser4 56⚠︎.
    DomainSet-LapsADPasswordExpirationTime -Identity <computer>57⚠︎
  • P1
    Enabled local accounts are known and password-protected: Get-LocalUser | ? Enabled | ft Name,PasswordRequired,LastLogon4 → Disable-LocalUser <name>56⚠︎ for the rest. With domain policy alone, the workstations past the hands-on sample take this cut-off from the workstation baseline on the day: a Group Policy Preferences Local Users and Groups item for each account the sample flags, action Update with "Account is disabled" checked (Update also creates that account, disabled, on a host that lacks it).
  • P1
    End the old team's live sessions: quser35⚠︎ → logoff <ID>58⚠︎; file servers Close-SmbSession -ClientUserName '<DOMAIN\user>' -Force59⚠︎. With domain policy alone, the workstation baseline ends the sessions on the workstations past the hands-on sample on the day: a Group Policy Preferences immediate task, set to apply once, with item-level targeting that leaves out the hands-on sample's computers (a Computer Name item set to Is Not for each, joined with AND), restarts each workstation past the sample at its next policy refresh, which signs every user out, so tell the staff first. The old team's domain accounts are disabled earlier in this phase and the listed local accounts by the step above, so they stay signed out.
  • P1
    Remote-control tools the old team could reach you through (installed programs and services):
    $rx='AnyDesk|ScreenConnect|ConnectWise|TeamViewer|Splashtop|Atera|NetSupport|Remote ?Utilities|RemotePC|Kaseya|N-?able|Pulseway|GoTo|LogMeIn|Zoho|BeyondTrust|Bomgar|SimpleHelp|JWrapper|RustDesk|Ninja|Radmin|VNC|ngrok'⚠︎
    Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*,HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*,Registry::HKEY_USERS\*\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -EA 0 | ? DisplayName -match $rx | ft DisplayName,InstallDate60⚠︎
    Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | ? { "$($_.Name) $($_.DisplayName) $($_.PathName)" -match $rx } | ft Name,State,PathName61⚠︎
    Get-Process | ? { "$($_.Name) $($_.Path)" -match $rx } | ft Name,Id,Path62⚠︎
    → uninstall each one the owner leaves out (winget uninstall --name '<name>'63⚠︎, or Settings > Apps64); portable copies show only as processes, so delete their folders too. A sanctioned tool gets a new account in your name. With domain policy alone, the workstation baseline cuts the tools the sample finds off the network on the workstations past it on the day, and the week-1 plan uninstalls them: an inbound and an outbound Windows Defender Firewall block rule for each of the tool's program paths (its service and its client). A block rule overrides allow rules (all but authenticated-bypass ones, set to override block rules), so it also stops the inbound allow rules a tool's installer added; it holds on every Windows edition and covers a tool's service that runs as SYSTEM; an AppLocker deny rule, enforced on every Windows 11 edition once the Application Identity service starts automatically, covers such a service only with services enforcement set in its policy XML.
  • P1
    SSH server keys (Server 2025 ships the SSH server): Get-Service sshd -EA 07⚠︎; keep only the keys you can attribute in C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys and C:\Users\*\.ssh\authorized_keys.

6 · Policy and visibility

Domain: the audit, log, credential-theft, and UAC settings suit every host, so they go in a new GPO, "Takeover Baseline", linked at the domain (GUI+ gpmc.msc71; it reaches every host at the next refresh). Workgroup hosts take the lines host by host or through remote shells.

  • P1
    Password and lockout (14 characters; length beats complexity, and changes follow events, such as today's):
    Set-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy <domain> -MinPasswordLength 14 -ComplexityEnabled $true -PasswordHistoryCount 24 -MinPasswordAge 1.00:00:00 -MaxPasswordAge 365.00:00:00 -LockoutThreshold 5 -LockoutDuration 00:30:00 -LockoutObservationWindow 00:30:00 -ReversibleEncryptionEnabled $false94⚠︎
    Localnet accounts /minpwlen:14 /uniquepw:24 /minpwage:1 /maxpwage:36595⚠︎
    Localnet accounts /lockoutthreshold:5 /lockoutduration:30 /lockoutwindow:3096⚠︎
  • P2
    Fine-grained password policies override the domain policy for their groups; each one meets the same floor: Get-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Filter * | ft Name,MinPasswordLength,AppliesTo97⚠︎.

    auditpol --% /set /subcategory:"Security Group Management","Process Creation","Special Logon","Audit Policy Change","Authentication Policy Change" /success:enable98⚠︎

    Credential-theft guards: LSA protection (1 = with UEFI lock; 2 = without, Windows 11) → after the restart, System log WinInit event 12 reads "protected process"; WDigest off keeps passwords out of memory:
    reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v RunAsPPL /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f92⚠︎
    reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest /v UseLogonCredential /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f92⚠︎
  • P1
    UAC on: reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v EnableLUA39 → 0x1.
  • P2
    Time: the PDC emulator syncs to the agreed source; others follow the domain.
    w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:"<ntp>" /syncfromflags:manual /reliable:yes /update; w32tm /resync99⚠︎
  • P2
    NTLMv2 only, after the Security log shows the old devices are gone: reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v LmCompatibilityLevel /t REG_DWORD /d 5 /f92⚠︎.
  • P2
    Potentially unwanted apps blocked: Set-MpPreference -PUAProtection Enabled67⚠︎.
  • P2
    Sysmon with a vetted config: Windows 11 (Feb 2026 update and later) has it built in, off by default; servers use the standalone Sysmon100 download (remove one before installing the other).
    Win11Get-Service sysmon*7⚠︎→ empty; a standalone copy comes off first (sysmon64 -u100⚠︎), since the two run one at a time
    Win11Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Sysmon101⚠︎
    CMDDism /Online /Enable-Feature /FeatureName:Sysmon102⚠︎(the same feature from a cmd window)
    Win11sysmon -i <config.xml>103⚠︎
    → Windows Server 2025 carries built-in Sysmon104 too, so on those servers these lines take the place of the standalone download.
  • P2
    DCs still issuing RC4 tickets: System log KDCSVC events 201–209 name the accounts and services (DCs default to AES since the April 2026 update).

7 · Recovery readiness

  • P1
    GUI+ Backup console: last good job per server, an offline or immutable copy, and console logins in your team's names only. Windows Server Backup105: wbadmin get versions106⚠︎.
  • P2
    System-state backup of one DC now: wbadmin start systemstatebackup -backupTarget:<E:> -quiet107⚠︎.
  • P2
    Restore one file from last night's job to an alternate folder.

8 · Verify, freeze, hand off

From the freeze, verify and log only.

  • P1
    Read-backs per host, compared with Phase 1:
    Get-LocalGroupMember -SID S-1-5-32-544; Get-NetFirewallProfile | ft Name,Enabled,DefaultInboundAction52 76
    cd C:\takeover; Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Export-Csv listen-after.csv -NoType; Compare-Object (Import-Csv listen.csv).LocalPort (Import-Csv listen-after.csv).LocalPort6 108⚠︎
    DomainGet-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins'; Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy; auditpol /get /category:*22 109 110⚠︎
    Get-NetIPAddress | ft InterfaceIndex,IPAddress,PrefixLength,InterfaceAlias -Auto15⚠︎
    Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | ft LocalAddress,LocalPort,OwningProcess -Auto6⚠︎
  • P1
    The owner confirms each required service with a real user: sign-in, file shares, apps, printing, and remote access.
  • P1
    Restarts for updates, LSA protection, and features: one server at a time, DCs one at a time, inside the window; recheck required services after each.
  • P1
    Hand off: change log, vault entries, findings, and the week-1 plan; then Stop-Transcript111⚠︎.

Week-1 plan

  • P3
    krbtgt reset 2 of 2, at least 10 hours after reset 1 and after replication.
  • P3
    Windows LAPS on every server and on each host the workstation baseline left out; separate admin accounts per tier; admins in Protected Users; MFA for remote access and email.
  • P3
    Group Managed Service Accounts for services; retire unsupported systems; a monthly patch cadence.
  • P3
    The vendor's security baseline for each Windows version, piloted in one OU; attack surface reduction rules; Credential Guard; BitLocker with escrowed keys; Administrator protection on Windows 11 desktops outside LAPS.
  • P3
    Secure Boot 2023 certificates on every host before the 2011 ones expire: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecureBoot\Servicing → UEFICA2023Status = Updated (System log event 1808).
  • P3
    Central log collection (Windows Event Forwarding or a SIEM); rerun the Phase 4 domain checks and track each finding to closed.
  • P3
    Workstations past the hands-on sample: the Phase 1 and 4 evidence and hunting steps; where domain policy alone reached them, also the steps it leaves to this plan: the snapshots (taken after the baseline, so they record its result; the sample's snapshots, taken before it, show what it changed), the Windows Update check, the Defender signature update and scan, the Phase 3 reads (live sessions, local accounts, and remote-control tools) with uninstalling the tools the baseline blocks, the custom inbound-rule review, roles and features removal, and read-backs. Each goes host by host or from the reach runs' collected output, with each finding tracked to closed.

Experimental: a starting point for your own judgment. Vendor documentation and your rehearsals decide. Rehearse on lab machines before you run these on a network you're responsible for.

*nix Takeover Checklist

Debian 12 / 13 and derivatives · RHEL 9 / 10 and Fedora · SLES 15 / 16, openSUSE Leap, and Tumbleweed · FreeBSD 14.x / 15.x · OpenBSD 7.9 / 8.0 · OpenIndiana Hipster and OmniOS · Oracle Solaris 11.4 · macOS 26 / 27. For the *nix cell of a takeover team (a team lead plus one or more people per cell; a cell of three or more names a cell lead) inheriting a network whose last admin team left under a negligence finding.

Situation. Treat every secret the old team held as known to outsiders, and every setting as unreviewed. Pick the host's family with the family switch, or print that family's copy; each step then shows that family's lines. Run each line in a root shell.

Debian Root shell: sudo -i1⚠︎, or su -2⚠︎ on hosts installed with a root password (those ship without sudo).

RHEL Root shell: sudo -i1⚠︎ as a member of wheel.

SUSE Root shell: sudo -i1⚠︎ or su -2⚠︎. On 15.x and on upgraded hosts, sudo asks for root's password; fresh 16.x and Tumbleweed installs (sudo-policy-wheel-auth-self) ask wheel members for their own.

FreeBSD Root shell: su -2⚠︎; when echo $0⚠︎ names csh or tcsh (hosts upgraded from 13.x keep it), run exec env SHELL=/bin/sh /bin/sh -l3⚠︎ first, since every FreeBSD line is written for sh.

OpenBSD Root shell: su -l2⚠︎ as a member of wheel, or doas -s4⚠︎ where doas.conf permits it; root's shell is ksh, and every OpenBSD line is written for sh and ksh.

illumos Root shell: su -2⚠︎; root's login shell is bash on OpenIndiana and OmniOS, and every illumos line also runs in ksh93.

Solaris Root shell: su -2⚠︎ (root is a role: each admin who holds it signs in as themselves, then assumes it); every Solaris line runs in bash and ksh93.

macOS Root shell: sudo -i1⚠︎ as an admin, while the root account stays disabled; Phase 1 gives Terminal Full Disk Access first.

Labels: Debian = Debian 12/13 and derivatives · RHEL = RHEL 9/10 and Fedora · SUSE = SLES 15/16, openSUSE Leap, and Tumbleweed · FreeBSD = FreeBSD 14/15 · OpenBSD = OpenBSD 7.9/8.0 · illumos = OpenIndiana Hipster and OmniOS · Solaris = Oracle Solaris 11.4 · macOS = macOS 26/27 · Linux = the three Linux families · BSD = FreeBSD and OpenBSD · Unix = illumos and Solaris. In All, a badge names each line's family, and a line without a badge fits every family.

Solo: internet-facing servers first, P1 lines in order, P2 when on schedule. Cell of two or more: split the hosts in the Hosts bar by family (Linux and FreeBSD, say) or by role (servers and desktops), each person with the switch set to the family of the host in front of them; each reads the line aloud, logs the change, and checks the → read-back. A cell of three or more names a cell lead, who sends the cell's roll-up to the team lead.

Key: P1 = inside the team clock · P2 = when on schedule · P3 = week-1 plan · → = expected read-back · <x> = your value · GUI+ = the GUI is faster here · ⚠︎ and an orange bar = untested on a real system: use with caution, at your own risk · a line without them = run cleanly on a real system.

Rules: evidence before change · lock before delete · a console session (VM console or BMC) stays open for any SSH, PAM, sudo, or firewall change · keep every required service running · one change, one log line (time, host, change, old → new, undo).

1 · Evidence and safety net (read-only)

  • P1
    A second root shell stays open until the end: your way back after an SSH, PAM, or sudo mistake.
    Unix → the system console counts as that second shell, and it is also the way back after an RBAC mistake.
    macOS → macOS keeps the root account disabled, so the way back is a second admin Terminal with sudo -i1⚠︎ open, or the recovery environment (the console password unlocks it). sudo -i1⚠︎ starts root's own /bin/sh, where every macOS line here runs as written; in a zsh shell (sudo -s1⚠︎ keeps the admin's zsh), run setopt nonomatch5⚠︎ first, since zsh otherwise stops a whole line when one of its wildcards matches nothing.
    macOS → before the snapshot, give Terminal Full Disk Access (System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access) and log that change in the session log: with it, root's reads of protected folders under /Users, the privacy database, and the logs come back whole.

    OpenBSD → the safety net is a VM snapshot (FFS keeps one live copy of each file); on bare metal, the snapshot block's etc.tgz and /var/backups (security(8)16's copies of each file in /etc/changelist17, run nightly by daily(8)) hold the configuration, and /altroot holds yesterday's root file system where /etc/daily.local sets ROOTBACKUP=1 and /etc/fstab carries an altroot line.
    illumos → a boot environment copies the root file system, /var included; /export (homes) and other pools stay outside it, so a VM snapshot stays first choice for data.
    Solaris → beadm list12⚠︎ shows pre-takeover, and zfs list -t snapshot -r rpool/export rpool/VARSHARE18⚠︎ shows the home and shared /var snapshots. A boot environment holds the OS datasets alone, so data pools stay outside it and a VM snapshot stays first choice for data.
    macOS → an APFS local snapshot you can restore from in the recovery environment; a Time Machine backup to an external disk is the fuller restore point and stays first choice for data.

    Linux → auth.txt holds sign-ins and sudo use from the journal (facilities auth and authpriv); boots.txt lists more than one boot where the journal keeps history on disk.
    Linux → /tmp empties at reboot on hosts that keep it in memory (Debian 13 also ages out old files in /tmp and /var/tmp), so copy anything odd from tmp.txt into this folder before the Phase 8 reboot.
    FreeBSD → /tmp empties at the Phase 8 reboot once Phase 6 sets clear_tmp_enable, so copy anything odd from tmp.txt into this folder before then.
    OpenBSD → in sockets.txt a line with an arrow (<-- or -->, or <==, ==>, and <==> for spliced sockets) is a connection and a line without one is a listener; the copied mailbox named root holds the nightly daily(8) and security(8)16 reports, the host's own record of changed accounts, SUID files, and configuration files (where /etc/mail/aliases or /root/.forward sends root's mail to a local account, copy that account's /var/mail file too); authlog holds SSH sign-ins and secure holds doas use.
    OpenBSD → daily(8) clears old files from /tmp each night, so copy anything odd from tmp.txt into this folder now.
    illumos → stock syslog writes errors to /var/adm/messages and sends auth notices to the console alone, so SSH sign-ins live in last25⚠︎ (wtmpx) and su attempts in /var/adm/sulog; the Phase 6 syslog step adds an auth.info line that writes /var/log/authlog. The tar archive holds relative paths, so a later extract lands where you run it. /tmp is a swap-backed filesystem that empties at the Phase 8 reboot, so copy anything odd from tmp.txt into this folder before then.
    Solaris → net.txt holds every listener and connection with its user, PID, and program (netstat -u), ps.txt names each process's zone, and svc-cust.txt lists each local change to a service. SSH sign-ins reach /var/adm/messages or authlog only where syslog takes auth.info (Phase 6 adds it), so the audit folder and sulog carry the sign-in record; a p_dir other than /var/audit in audit-config.txt names a folder to copy too.
    Solaris → /tmp lives in swap and empties at the Phase 8 reboot, so copy anything odd from tmp.txt into this folder before then.
    macOS → /etc and /tmp are links to /private/etc and /private/tmp, so tar and find name the real folders; /private/var/db/dslocal holds the local account records, including password hashes, so etc.tgz is a secret; auth.txt is the unified log, where macOS records sign-ins, sudo use, and screen-sharing sessions (system.log stays mostly empty); the log line runs last and takes a few minutes, so let it finish before the evidence hashes.

    macOS → macOS verifies its base system through the signed system volume (checked in Phase 4), so this slow background scan checks the signatures of installed apps and third-party binaries in the form Gatekeeper uses, and Phase 4 reads codesign.txt; open the other terminal with sudo -i1⚠︎ too, so a wildcard that matches nothing stays harmless.

    Commands resolve to the system's own copies before anyone types a password (a planted wrapper, alias, function, or trap earlier in root's shell captures what you type):
    Linuxtype -a passwd sudo su usermod chage visudo sshd; alias; echo "$PATH"; echo "$PROMPT_COMMAND"; trap -p; ls -la /usr/local/sbin /usr/local/bin /root/bin 2>/dev/null3⚠︎
    FreeBSDfor c in passwd su pw chpass visudo sshd sudo doas; do type "$c"; done; alias; echo "$PATH"; trap; ls -la /usr/local/sbin /usr/local/bin /root/bin 2>/dev/null3⚠︎
    OpenBSDfor c in passwd su usermod chpass vipw doas sshd sudo visudo; do type "$c"; done; alias; echo "$PATH"; echo "$PS1"; echo "$ENV"; trap; ls -la /usr/local/sbin /usr/local/bin /root/bin 2>/dev/null3⚠︎
    illumosfor c in passwd su sudo pfexec profiles roles visudo sshd; do type "$c"; done; alias; echo "$PATH"; trap; ls -l /usr/local/sbin /usr/local/bin /root/bin 2>/dev/null3⚠︎
    Solarisfor c in passwd su sudo pfexec usermod roles profiles visudo; do type "$c"; done; alias; echo "$PATH"; trap; ls -la /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin /root/bin 2>/dev/null3⚠︎
    macOSfor c in passwd su sudo visudo sshd dscl; do type "$c"; done; alias; echo "$PATH"; trap; ls -la /usr/local/sbin /usr/local/bin /opt/homebrew/bin /var/root/bin 2>/dev/null; cat /etc/paths /etc/paths.d/* 2>/dev/null3⚠︎
    Linux → each name resolves to /usr/bin or /usr/sbin (or /bin and /sbin), and the alias, PROMPT_COMMAND, and trap lists hold stock entries alone.
    FreeBSD → each name resolves to /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, or /usr/sbin (sudo and doas to /usr/local/bin, which pkg which82⚠︎ attributes), and the alias and trap lists hold stock entries alone.
    OpenBSD → each name resolves to /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, or /usr/sbin (sudo and visudo, where the package is installed, to /usr/local/bin and /usr/local/sbin, which pkg_info -E <path>46⚠︎ attributes); PS1 and ENV read the stock values or empty (ksh runs any command substitution in PS1 at every prompt); the alias and trap lists hold stock entries alone.
    illumos → each name resolves to /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, or /sbin (sshd to /usr/sbin, sudo and pfexec94⚠︎ to /usr/bin), and the alias and trap lists hold stock entries alone.
    Solaris → each name resolves to /usr/bin or /usr/sbin, PATH holds /usr/bin and /usr/sbin ahead of every other folder (a /usr/gnu/bin ahead of them swaps in GNU tools, which read these lines differently), and the alias and trap lists hold stock entries alone.
    macOS → each name resolves to /usr/bin or /usr/sbin, and the alias and trap lists hold stock entries alone; /etc/paths and each /etc/paths.d file (path_helper builds every login shell's PATH from them) list stock or approved folders; a third-party package-manager folder (/usr/local/bin or /opt/homebrew/bin) that shadows a system tool is a finding.

Week-1 plan

  • P3
    Central logging; SSH keys only, through a bastion with MFA; one configuration-management tool so hosts stay identical.
  • P3
    A host audit tool for a ranked follow-up list, and a file-integrity baseline:
    Debian → the packaged aide builds the baseline (aideinit346⚠︎).
    RHEL → dnf install aide && aide --init33 347⚠︎, then move /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz to aide.db.gz; application allow-listing (fapolicyd), a USB device policy (usbguard), and a boot-loader password (grub2-setpassword348⚠︎) round out the plan.
    SUSE → zypper in aide && aide --init && mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db37 347 168⚠︎, then aide --check347⚠︎ reads the baseline (16.x and Tumbleweed: systemctl enable --now aide.timer24⚠︎ runs it daily; 15.x: copy the package's example /usr/share/doc/packages/aide/examples/etc/cron.daily/aide.sh into /etc/cron.daily/). Setting PERMISSION_SECURITY="secure local" in /etc/sysconfig/security and running chkstat --system --set221⚠︎ drops SUID from some tools, so test it first.
    FreeBSD → mtree for the baseline; FreeBSD securelevel once updates settle.
    OpenBSD → security(8)16, run nightly by daily(8), mails root the setuid changes and the diffs of /etc/changelist and /etc/mtree/special; a baseline per tree joins that run: mtree -cx -p /bin -K sha256digest,type > /etc/mtree/bin.secure86⚠︎, then /sbin, /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, and /usr/local/bin, each followed by chmod 600301⚠︎. Securelevel 2286 stays aside while pf rules still change, since it freezes them.
    illumos → BART builds the file-integrity baseline: bart create > <manifest>349⚠︎ catalogs the root file system, and a later manifest with bart compare <control> <test>349⚠︎ lists each change; pkg verify52⚠︎ checks every packaged file against its package.
    Solaris → pkg install security/compliance178⚠︎, then compliance assess -b solaris -p Recommended -a week1350⚠︎ and compliance report -a week1350⚠︎ rank the follow-up list; bart create -R /etc > /root/takeover/bart-etc.manifest349⚠︎ records the file-integrity baseline (bart compare349⚠︎ reads a later manifest against it), and pkg verify52⚠︎ checks every packaged file.
    macOS → the signed system volume seals the OS itself (csrutil authenticated-root status63⚠︎ reads enabled); mtree -c -K sha256digest -p /Library > /var/root/takeover/library.mtree86⚠︎ and mtree -c -K sha256digest -p /private/etc > /var/root/takeover/etc.mtree86⚠︎ baseline the writable trees; copy both to the evidence store, and the week-1 plan compares /private/etc against that copy each week (mtree -f <evidence-store>/etc.mtree -p /private/etc86⚠︎ names each changed file, sudoers and pam.d included). A firmware password (Intel) or Recovery Lock (Apple silicon, set through MDM) keeps recoveryOS for the team.
  • P3
    Linux · macOS Hosts with mandatory access control disabled come back to enforcing, one host at a time with the owner's sign-off:
    RHEL · SUSE → SELinux: SELINUX=permissive in /etc/selinux/config, clear selinux=0 from the boot flags, fixfiles -F onboot344⚠︎, reboot (the relabel is slow), read the AVCs, then enforcing.
    SUSE → SELinux on SUSE also needs update-bootloader --add-option security=selinux315⚠︎ and update-bootloader --add-option selinux=1315⚠︎, then update-bootloader --config315⚠︎.
    Debian · SUSE → AppArmor: clear apparmor=0 (and any lsm= list that leaves apparmor out) from the boot flags, reboot, then aa-enforce312⚠︎ each profile the owner's tests pass.
    macOS → System Integrity Protection: start up in recoveryOS (Apple silicon: hold the power button; Intel: Command-R), open Terminal there, run csrutil enable63⚠︎, then restart; csrutil status63⚠︎ reads enabled. Authenticated Root disabled: in recoveryOS run csrutil authenticated-root enable63⚠︎, and boot the last sealed snapshot (bless --mount <system volume> --last-sealed-snapshot351⚠︎) once the owner has saved any change made to the system volume; csrutil authenticated-root status63⚠︎ then reads enabled. An unapproved boot-args clears with nvram -d boot-args219⚠︎ from recoveryOS; nvram boot-args219⚠︎ then reads empty or approved.
  • P3
    Linux Root locked with passwd -l root119⚠︎ once the Phase 8 reboot came back clean and each admin passes sudo -v1⚠︎; from then on a failed boot recovers through the boot loader's kernel line:
    RHEL · SUSE → append rd.break157 to the kernel line (dracut), then mount -o remount,rw /sysroot; chroot /sysroot158 159⚠︎; SELinux hosts finish the repair with touch /.autorelabel160⚠︎ before exit3⚠︎, so files changed there get their labels at the next boot (slow on large disks).
    Debian → append init=/bin/bash to the kernel line, then mount -o remount,rw /158⚠︎; or append break=bottom for the initramfs shell, then mount -o remount,rw /root; chroot /root158 159⚠︎.
    SUSE → first rpm -q sudo-policy-wheel-auth-self32⚠︎ names the package (otherwise zypper in sudo-policy-wheel-auth-self37⚠︎, which also brings the wheel group), each admin sits in wheel, and each admin passes sudo -v1⚠︎ with their own password; with root locked, the stock ALL ALL138 line stops granting sudo.
  • P3
    illumos Root becomes a role (OpenIndiana does this at install when it creates a user; OmniOS keeps root as a sign-in account) once the Phase 8 reboot came back clean, with the root shell kept open until a second admin session passes su - root2⚠︎ with root's vault password. First, grep -v '^#' /root/.ssh/authorized_keys⚠︎ and the owner list every job that signs in as root (backup pulls, zfs send pipelines, and configuration tools); each moves to a service account with the needed profile before root becomes a role, since a role takes sign-ins only through su, SSH keys included. A failed boot then recovers in single-user mode (boot -s165⚠︎ at the loader prompt), which still takes root's password (the Phase 6 PASSREQ read covers /etc/default/sulogin321):
    usermod -K type=role root126⚠︎
    usermod -R root <admin>126⚠︎(each admin; -R replaces the admin's role list, so name every role they hold)
    Readroles <admin>; grep '^root:' /etc/user_attr144⚠︎→ root; type=role; a second session passes su - root as each admin
    Undorolemod -K type=normal root318⚠︎
  • P3
    Solaris Root stays a role (the stock setting): each admin signs in as themselves and assumes it with su -2⚠︎, and a failed boot recovers in single-user mode with root's vault password:
    Readuserattr type root; getent user_attr | grep 'roles=.*root'352 23⚠︎→ role, then the approved admins alone
    → usermod -K type=role root126⚠︎ turns root back into a role; usermod -R +root <admin>126⚠︎ adds the root role to an approved admin's roles, and usermod -R -root <user>126⚠︎ removes it from an unapproved one.
  • P3
    Patch cadence and release upgrades:
    Debian → unattended-upgrades verified (unattended-upgrade --dry-run --debug118⚠︎); Debian 12 hosts move to 13 before long-term support ends June 30, 2028.
    RHEL → the automatic timer verified; Fedora hosts move up before end of life (dnf system-upgrade download --releasever=<N>353⚠︎, then dnf system-upgrade reboot353⚠︎).
    SUSE → the 15.x online-update job or the 16.x os-update.timer354⚠︎ verified; SP6 hosts move to SP7 (zypper migration355⚠︎), and Leap 15.6 hosts move to Leap 16.0 with the distribution's migration tool.
    FreeBSD → freebsd-update cron83⚠︎ plus weekly pkg upgrade105⚠︎.
    OpenBSD → syspatch45⚠︎ and pkg_add -u107⚠︎ run on a schedule from root's crontab (syspatch -c45⚠︎ lists pending patches and suits cron). Errata reach the two most recent releases and package fixes the latest alone110, so 7.9 hosts move to 8.0 with sysupgrade111⚠︎ soon, and 8.0 hosts move to 8.1 within six months of its release. syspatch covers amd64, i386, and arm64; hosts on other architectures follow the source patches on the errata page. sysupgrade111⚠︎ reboots as soon as it finishes, so sysupgrade -n111⚠︎ stages the upgrade for a planned reboot.
    illumos → OmniOS: weekly pkg update104⚠︎, and a new stable release each May and November (Nov 2026: r151060 stable, r151058 until May 3, 2027, and r151054 LTS); r151056 left support on Nov 2, 2026, so its hosts move up first. Before the upgrade, sshd -t151⚠︎ passes (sshd starts on the new release once legacy options are gone), ipkg-branded zones are detached (zoneadm -z <zone> detach54⚠︎), and the session's evidence is copied off the host, since the new boot environment leaves out changes made after the update starts. Then beadm create <backup-name>12⚠︎, pkg set-publisher -r -O https://pkg.omnios.org/r151060/core omnios356⚠︎ (and the extra.omnios publisher the same way), pkg update -f -r --be-name=r151060104⚠︎, and a reboot. OpenIndiana Hipster rolls forward: pkg update104⚠︎, then a reboot into the new boot environment.
    Solaris → SRUs arrive monthly from the support repository that pkg publisher52⚠︎ names; pkg update -nv104⚠︎ previews the next one, and each lands in a new boot environment, live at the next reboot.
    macOS → the Phase 2 automatic-update settings verified; the 9 Nov 2026 security release357 covered macOS 27, 26, and 15, so a host on 14 or older goes on the plan as an upgrade.
  • P3
    Desktop browser policies (managed-policy files); password aging per policy.
    Solaris → password aging lives in account-policy206 (password/aging_defaults/max_days, min_days, and warn_days) once its passwd stencil is on; passwd -x <days> <user>119⚠︎ sets aging on each existing account.
    macOS → configuration profiles carry browser policies; password aging joins the account policy file as a policyCategoryPasswordChange rule.
  • P3
    Workstations past the hands-on sample: the Phase 1 and 4 evidence and hunting steps, host by host or from the reach runs' collected output, each finding tracked to closed.
    macOS → each admin's own password change at their next sign-in (Phase 3) is tracked here until every admin has made it.

Experimental: a starting point for your own judgment. Vendor documentation and your rehearsals decide. Rehearse on lab machines before you run these on a network you're responsible for.

Cisco IOS / IOS XE Takeover Checklist

Routers and Catalyst switches · IOS 15.x · IOS XE 17.x. For the network cell of a takeover team (a team lead plus one or more people per cell; a cell of three or more names a cell lead) inheriting a network whose last admin team left under a negligence finding.

Situation. Treat every secret the old team held as known to outsiders, and every setting as unreviewed. Lines that start with show, dir, copy, verify, clear, reload, more, terminal, configure, or guestshell, plus no monitor capture1⚠︎, run at the # prompt; the rest run in configure terminal2⚠︎. Indented lines run in the mode the line above opened.

Solo: edge router first, then core, then access switches; P1 lines in order, P2 when on schedule. Cell of two or more: split the devices in the Hosts bar, one person on the routers and the edge and the others on the switches; each person reads the line aloud, logs the change, and checks the → read-back. A cell of three or more names a cell lead, who sends the cell's roll-up to the team lead.

Key: P1 = inside the team clock · P2 = when on schedule · P3 = week-1 plan · → = expected read-back · <x> = your value · GUI+ = the GUI is faster here · ⚠︎ and an orange bar = untested on a real system: use with caution, at your own risk · a line without them = run cleanly on a real system.

Rules: evidence before change · a console session stays open for any VTY, ACL, AAA, or trunk change · keep every required link and service running · save each device after each phase · one change, one log line (time, device, change, old → new, undo).

1 · Access and evidence (read-only)

  • P1
    Console or out-of-band access to every device. A device without working credentials gets password recovery, inside the window.
  • P1
    GUI+ Turn on your terminal program's session logging (all output) before the first command; the log files are your evidence and your change record.
  • P1
    Evidence block, pasted per device:
    terminal length 03⚠︎show version4⚠︎show running-config5⚠︎show startup-config6⚠︎show users7⚠︎show ip interface brief8⚠︎show ip route9⚠︎show access-lists10⚠︎show logging11⚠︎show clock detail12⚠︎show cdp neighbors detail13⚠︎show archive14⚠︎dir15⚠︎
    show ip arp16⚠︎show lldp neighbors detail17⚠︎show standby brief18⚠︎show ip dhcp binding19⚠︎show running-config | include ip helper-address5⚠︎
    Routershow ip nat translations · show crypto session · show interfaces summary20 21 22⚠︎
    Switchshow vlan brief · show interfaces trunk · show vtp status · show monitor session all23 24 25 26⚠︎
    Switchshow mac address-table dynamic · show interfaces status · show etherchannel summary · show spanning-tree root · show ip dhcp snooping binding27 28 29 30 31⚠︎
  • P1
    Copies before any change: copy running-config flash:takeover-before.cfg32⚠︎, and off the device copy running-config scp://<user>@<host>/<device>-before.cfg32⚠︎.
  • P1
    Running image matches the vendor's published hash: show version | include System image4⚠︎ → verify /sha512 <fs:image>33⚠︎ (install mode: each .pkg listed by more flash:packages.conf34⚠︎); IOS XE also show software authenticity running35⚠︎. A mismatch: collect evidence before any reload, isolate, and escalate.
  • P1
    Record signs of misuse (unknown privilege-15 users, outside hosts in ACLs, SNMP RW strings, tunnels, mirror sessions) and escalate per policy before fixing.

2 · Safety net and prepared blocks

  • P1
    Rollback timer before each remote change. Once per device: archive36⚠︎ → path flash:archive37⚠︎. Each session: configure terminal revert timer 102⚠︎, make the change, verify, then configure confirm38⚠︎ (test the timer once on one device). Backstop on any platform, while the change is unsaved: reload in 1039⚠︎ before, reload cancel39⚠︎ after (decline any save prompt).
  • P1
    GUI+ Fill in the Phase 3, 5, and 6 blocks once in a text editor (admin name, management subnets, NTP, syslog), then paste them per device; pasting beats retyping on every box.

3 · Cut off the old team

  • P1
    Live sessions: show users7⚠︎ → clear line vty <n>40⚠︎ for each session outside your team.
  • P1
    Accounts: show running-config | include ^username5⚠︎ → no username <u>41⚠︎ for each name off the approved list, privilege 15 first. Names such as cisco_tac_admin or cisco_support, or log lines from SEP_webui_wsma_http, point to the exploited web UI implant (CVE-2023-20198): isolate and escalate.
  • P1
    New secrets, hashed with scrypt (Type 9); the length floor goes first:
    security passwords min-length 1442⚠︎(classic IOS; IOS XE releases without it rely on vault-generated length)
    enable algorithm-type scrypt secret <new>43⚠︎
    no enable password44⚠︎
    username <admin> privilege 15 algorithm-type scrypt secret <new>41⚠︎
  • P1
    SSH v2 with a fresh, named key, before any line goes SSH-only (hostname and domain come first; older IOS writes ip domain-name45⚠︎; a new label avoids the replace prompt that would swallow the next pasted line):
    hostname <name>46⚠︎
    ip domain name <domain>45⚠︎
    crypto key generate rsa general-keys label SSH-KEY modulus 307247⚠︎
    ip ssh rsa keypair-name SSH-KEY48⚠︎
    ip ssh version 248⚠︎

4 · Hunt persistence

  • P1
    Scripts and schedulers: show running-config | section event manager|kron|scripting tcl5⚠︎ and show event manager policy registered62⚠︎ → no event manager applet <name>63⚠︎ for each unknown applet; no kron occurrence <name>64⚠︎ likewise.

  • P1

  • P1
    Routes, port forwards, and ACL permits match the required list: show running-config | include ^ip route|ip nat inside source static5⚠︎ and show access-lists10⚠︎ → remove orphans. Edit ACLs by sequence number (ip access-list extended <name>55⚠︎ → no <seq>), since no access-list <n>70⚠︎ deletes the whole list.

  • P1

6 · Shrink the attack surface

Announce port and edge-ACL changes at the firewall and ACL sync; users feel these first.

  • P1
    Legacy services off; dead sessions reaped (IP phones that need CDP keep it: use no cdp enable98⚠︎ on the other ports instead of no cdp run99⚠︎):

8 · Verify, freeze, hand off

From the freeze, verify and log only.

  • P1
    show running-config | include password|secret|community|http server|transport input|vstack5⚠︎ → hashed secrets, SSH, and SNMPv3 only.
  • P1
    show running-config | section line vty5⚠︎ → every range has login local51⚠︎ (or AAA), transport input ssh52⚠︎, transport output none52⚠︎, access-class58⚠︎, and exec-timeout74⚠︎.
  • P1

  • P1

  • P1

    terminal length 03⚠︎show ip interface brief8⚠︎show ip route9⚠︎

  • P1
    Hand off: terminal logs, vault entries, findings, and the week-1 plan.

Keep running

Approved accounts, required links, and third-party devices stay as they are. Monitoring moves to SNMPv3 rather than going dark. IP phones keep CDP on their ports. aaa new-model90⚠︎ follows a working local privilege-15 user. The native VLAN stays free of users. The management ACL lists every management subnet, or remote admins lose access.

Week-1 plan

  • P3
    AAA through TACACS+ or RADIUS with MFA, per-admin accounts, and command accounting.
  • P3
    Upgrades to fixed releases; scheduled config backups; flow export to a collector.
  • P3
    Control-plane policing, uRPF at the edge, dynamic ARP inspection, 802.1X on user ports; certificate-based VPN in place of pre-shared keys.
